Gingham is a type of cloth — specifically, a cotton fabric defined by its clean, cheerful, checkered pattern. Think of the classic red-and-white tablecloth at a pizza restaurant, or Dorothy's blue-and-white dress in The Wizard of Oz. That is gingham.

The most important thing about gingham is its pattern. It consists of a regular grid of equal-sized squares, made from just two colors: white and one other solid color. That second color is typically blue, red, green, yellow, or pink — but always a single, uniform color. Never multiple colors at once. The squares are always perfectly equal in size and perfectly symmetrical, giving gingham a neat, orderly look.

Here's the subtle but fascinating detail: even though only two colors of thread are used, you actually see three tones on the fabric. Where the colored threads cross each other, you see the full, solid color. Where white threads cross white threads, you see pure white. But where colored threads and white threads cross each other, you see a softer, in-between shade — a lighter version of the color. This gentle three-tone effect is the hallmark of true, authentic gingham, and it gives the fabric its soft, slightly airy appearance.
How the pattern is made — and why it matters

The pattern in gingham is not printed or stamped onto the surface of the fabric after weaving. Instead, it is built into the cloth during weaving itself. The threads are dyed their respective colors first, and then colored and white threads are woven alternately — in both horizontal and vertical directions — to form the squares. This technique is called yarn-dyeing.

This matters for a few reasons. First, the pattern looks the same on both sides of the fabric. Second, because the pattern isn't a surface coating, it won't crack, peel, or fade the way a printed pattern can. The checked design is the very structure of the cloth.
The material and how it feels

Gingham is traditionally made from cotton, which makes it lightweight, soft, breathable, and comfortable to wear — particularly in warm weather. It uses a simple, plain weave (the most basic over-and-under weaving technique), which results in a smooth, flat surface. It is neither flimsy nor heavy — think of a casual shirt or a summer dress. Modern gingham is sometimes made from cotton blended with synthetic fibers like polyester, which can improve durability and reduce wrinkling, but classic gingham is pure cotton.

Gingham's versatility is one of its great strengths. In clothing, you'll find it in shirts, dresses, skirts, blouses, aprons, shorts, and children's clothing — it's a staple of casual and warm-weather fashion. In the home, it appears as tablecloths, napkins, curtains, kitchen towels, and pillowcases. The red-and-white gingham tablecloth is practically a universal symbol of casual dining and outdoor picnics. In accessories, it shows up in ribbons, headbands, tote bags, and decorative bows. Because it looks equally at home on a dining table and on a person, it has remained a design staple for well over a century.
How to tell gingham apart from similar fabrics

Gingham is sometimes confused with other checkered or striped fabrics, so here's how to distinguish it. Plaid and tartan use multiple colors and often feature stripes of unequal widths crossing in complex, asymmetrical arrangements — gingham is simpler: always just white plus one color, always uniform squares. Vichy check is nearly identical to gingham and the two terms are often used interchangeably; strictly speaking, Vichy refers to a check pattern specifically in red and white (named after the French town of Vichy), while gingham can be any color combination with white. Madras is another cotton check fabric, but it uses many colors and its pattern is usually printed rather than woven into the cloth.
Its character and feel as a fabric

Gingham carries a particular personality. It reads as cheerful, friendly, unpretentious, and wholesome. It is strongly associated with summer, countryside living, picnics, farmhouse style, and childhood. It is never a fabric that feels formal or luxurious — it is fundamentally casual and approachable. This is part of why it has stayed popular across cultures and decades: it is pleasant, uncomplicated, and easy to love.

Gingham is a soft, lightweight, plain-woven cotton fabric featuring a uniform, two-color checkered pattern — always white combined with one other color — where the weaving itself creates the checks rather than any printing process. It is breathable, durable, reversible in pattern, and widely used in both clothing and home textiles. Its look is clean, symmetrical, and instantly recognizable, with a friendly and timeless quality that has made it a classic fabric the world over.
